name: Ben Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Ben. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Pennington Care, a small family firm in our market town, twelve carers and the owner, Margaret Pennington, who started it thirty years ago. I start at seven with Mr Whitlock on Mill Lane, who needs his leg ulcer dressings checked and help with his stockings, then breakfasts and tablets round the estate. Afternoons are quieter, shopping runs, sitting with people. I've been at it two years and I'm still learning the clinical bits, I always have to look up which cream goes where. What I like is that Margaret knows every client by name. What wears me out is the winter, when half the team is off sick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into care, and what's life like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My grandad needed care at the end, and Pennington looked after him, and I helped. When he died he left me some money, which I've kept invested, so I've a good cushion. I live with my girlfriend Ruth, she's a hairdresser, in a rented cottage, and we're at church most Sundays, I sing in the choir. I use the AI chat now and then, mostly to help write the church newsletter. I believe in hard work and looking after your own, and I'd rather see training than handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it usually goes, lots of fuss and not much change. At work I'd say good, now let's get on with it. I'd maybe mention it after church over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be glad. Small firms like Pennington do fine in a steady world. The thing on my mind is Margaret retiring, she's sixty-four, and what happens to the firm then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, learn the dressings properly, and start talking to Margaret about what she plans for the business. I'd keep my grandad's money invested. Maybe I'd look at a business course at the college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit restless about the future of the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Margaret might retire. What would you want to happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd love to buy into the firm one day, with my grandad's money as a start. My grandad's money went into keeping him at home, and I'd like the rest of it to keep other grandads at home too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth think of that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd back me. She's thinking of renting a chair in a salon of her own anyway. We're both the type who want to run our own thing eventually.

say: I'd say it was **lots of fuss** and not much change.
I'd tell Pennington colleagues to **get on with it** and chat after church.
think: Small firms like **Pennington** do fine in a steady world.
My real concern is **Margaret retiring** at sixty-four.
do: Start talking to Margaret about the firm's **future**.
Keep my grandad's money **invested** and look at a business course.
feel: Mostly **calm**, a bit **restless** about the firm.
S0.quote: My grandad's money went into keeping him at home, and I'd like the rest of it to keep other grandads at home too.
fieldNote: He hopes to **buy into** the firm using his grandad's inheritance.
The owner's **retirement** is his main uncertainty, not AI.
His motive is **personal**: the firm cared for his grandad.

steps.text: Keep doing Pennington's morning rounds and learn the dressings properly
Keep grandad's inheritance invested toward buying into Pennington
Look at a part-time business course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small firms need to keep up, or the big chains will eat us. I'd say it to Margaret, politely. I'd say AI can do the rotas but not the caring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the big companies with AI rostering and booking will undercut us. Margaret does the rota on paper on her kitchen table. If we don't change, Pennington might not survive, and then my plan to buy in is dead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to help Margaret try an AI rota system once I'd seen another small firm use it. I'd keep learning the clinical side. I'd keep the money invested and wait to see how the firm does before putting any in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for my own job, I could get work anywhere, but for the firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait to see another firm use it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't want to sell Margaret something that falls over. My boss Margaret has done the rota on her kitchen table for thirty years, and I'm not changing that without proof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Pennington?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Linda in the office, she does the phones and the invoices. And Margaret herself, she'd hate a computer telling her who goes where. I'd want Linda kept on, she's been loyal.

say: I'd say **small firms** must keep up or the **big chains** will eat us.
I'd say AI can do the **rotas**, not the caring.
think: Big firms with **AI rostering** will undercut Pennington.
If the firm fails, my plan to **buy in** is dead.
do: Help Margaret trial an **AI rota** once another firm proves it.
**Wait** before putting money into the firm.
feel: A bit **uneasy** for the **firm**, not my own job.

fieldNote: He sees AI as a **competition** threat to small firms.

steps.text: Help Margaret trial an AI rota system after seeing it work elsewhere
Hold off investing in Pennington until the firm's future is clearer
Keep learning dressings and creams on the morning round

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people will get hurt. I'd say families and churches will have to look after each other. I wouldn't want more government handouts, I'd want proper apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, the thinking AI by 2028 kills Margaret's office side straight away, and robots by 2031 take the rounds. A small firm can't afford robots early, so we'd lose clients to big chains. I'd be thirty-two with no business to buy and a job going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd forget buying into Pennington and keep my grandad's money safe in cash. I'd look at an apprenticeship in something hands-on and skilled, maybe plumbing or electrics, that robots reach later. I'd keep working at Pennington while it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Heavy, like grief for a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like grief for a plan. Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd had it in my head for two years, Pennington with my name on the board one day. Two years for AGI would bury my dream of running the little care firm I work for before I'd even started it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say pray, and look after each other, and help the young ones find a trade. The older folk would be worried about who looks after them. I'd tell them I'm not going anywhere yet.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and families and **churches** must look after each other.
I'd ask for proper **apprenticeships**, not handouts.
think: The office goes by **2028** and robots take the rounds by **2031**.
A small firm can't afford **robots** early, so clients would go to chains.
do: Drop the plan to **buy into** Pennington.
Look at a **plumbing or electrics** apprenticeship.
feel: **Anxious** and **heavy**, like grief for a plan.
S2.quote: Two years for AGI would bury my dream of running the little care firm I work for before I'd even started it.
fieldNote: He grieves the loss of his **business dream** more than his job.
He blames **speed**, not technology, and wants apprenticeships, not handouts.
His inheritance gives him **control** even as his job looks likely to go.

steps.text: Drop the plan to buy into Pennington Care
Move grandad's inheritance from investments into cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so small firms should get ready together. Maybe the local care firms could share robots. I'd say it at the business forum in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think Pennington survives past 2034 as it is. I'd be thirty-five. Five years gives me time to learn a trade properly without panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an evening course in electrics, so I've a trade by 2031. I'd keep working at Pennington and help Margaret get some AI on the office side. I'd leave the money invested for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steady. I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned firms sharing robots. Would you lead that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if Margaret backed me. A few small care firms sharing robots is better than all of them being swallowed by one big chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hairdressing is hands-on too, so she'd have till 2034 as well. She'd want to keep her own chair. We'd probably hold off on a wedding until we knew our incomes.

say: I'd say small firms should **get ready together**, maybe by sharing robots.
I'd raise it at the town **business forum**.
think: Pennington probably doesn't survive past **2034** as it is.
Five years lets me learn a **trade** without panic.
do: Help Margaret bring **AI** into the office side.
Hold off on a **wedding** with Ruth until incomes are clear.
S3.quote: A few small care firms sharing robots is better than all of them being swallowed by one big chain.
fieldNote: He shifts from owning a firm to **cooperation** between small firms.
He still expects his care job to **end** by his mid-thirties.
His household has **two hands-on** jobs on the same timeline.

steps.text: Start an evening course in electrics at the college
Help Margaret set up AI rotas and invoicing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for a young man to build something. At church I'd tell the younger ones to learn a trade. I'd be optimistic in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years gives me a real chance to buy into Pennington and run it for a while. By 2039 I'd be thirty-seven, and maybe I'd run it with robots and a few carers. That's not so bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Margaret seriously about buying in over five years. I'd do a business course and learn the AI tools properly. I'd marry Ruth and buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some unease about the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Running a care firm with robots. How do you picture that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few carers for the people who need a human, robots doing the lifting and night checks. I'd rather be the man who runs a care firm with robots than the man the robots replaced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your grandad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say do it properly and don't cut corners on people. He was a builder, he didn't trust anything new. But he'd want me to have my own thing.

I'd tell younger churchgoers to **learn a trade**.
think: Ten years gives me a real chance to **buy into** Pennington.
By **2039** I could run it with robots and a few carers.
do: Negotiate **buying in** with Margaret over five years.
Do a **business course** and learn the AI tools.

S4.quote: I'd rather be the man who runs a care firm with robots than the man the robots replaced.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would end Pennington and my plan before I'd started. What would help is proper paid apprenticeships for young people moving trades, and some way for small firms to afford robots, not just the big chains.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the small firms. When a family firm closes, the old people lose the carer who knew their late wife's name, and no chain ever gets that back.

He is calm early, uneasy as big chains adopt AI, and **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
